newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling steady vs dlr, resists weakening.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling steady vs dlr, resists weakening.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling opened weaker against the dollar on Wednesday but resisted further pressure, signalling it had weathered the worst political violence in Kenya for seven years.

Forex dealers said they were trading within a narrow band of 58.50/59.40 against the dollar. The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) posted a shilling commercial mean of 58.98 against the dollar versus 58.78 on Tuesday. Against the pound, the central bank quoted the shilling at a mean of 98.77 from 99.27 on Tuesday.

Nine people were killed in battles between police and demonstrators last week. Market analysts said they believed the worst was over for the fragile Kenyan currency adding that President Daniel arap Moi's indication that he would start the process of dialogue over constitutional reforms was a positive indicator.

"Right now the most important thing is to restore investor confidence -- both monetary and political," said Abdalla Abdulkhalik, treasurer of Citibank NA. Violent political unrest last week sent the shilling to 61.50 on Friday from 55 at the beginning of the week.

The violence was sparked by calls, initially rejected by Moi, for constitutional reforms before elections this year. Moi met church leaders on Tuesday and parliamentary opposition leader Michael Wamalwa on Wednesday to discuss the question.

Abdulkhalik said the central bank had showed its commitment and ability to sustain a stable currency when it intervened to halt the shilling's further decline and calm a jittery market. CBK sold a total of $42 million in two days.
CBK Chief Economist Maurice Kanga said it could take some time for the shilling to return to levels of 55 where for a long time it had found support.
"It will all depend on the (political) developments. As long as there is a friendly environment, the shilling will be stable," Kanga told Reuters.
Charles Musau, senior dealer at the central bank, said the bank was comfortable with whatever levels the shilling settled at if they were determined by economic fundamentals.
Already, spreads have begun to thin -- a good sign the market was beginning to stabilise, Musau said.
Spreads were quoted between 50 cents and a shilling on Wednesday from as high as three shillings last week.
The test for the shilling will be Thursday's treasury bill auction, dealers said.

They said last week the central bank auctioned 5.074 billion shillings, well below the target of 11 billion. They said foreign investors declined to roll-over their treasury bills fearing continued political instability.
"Though all indications are for a positive outcome -- let's wait and see. It remains to be seen whether they'll roll over their bills," a dealer said.
